items.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023
items.q: You know I was his producer for a while, I produced six records for him.

ctx.x: It reminds me of, I had a conversation with Dave Frishberg and he said, “When I write I’m writing according to the limitations of my own vocal ability.” And then he said, “I bet Mose Allison would say the same thing. A lot of his songs are shaped by the way he sings.”

Yeah. I think that’s true. I know Mose also believed that he had to be playing piano in order to sing, that they were of one piece. You had to be sitting at the piano and accompanying himself when he sang.

Did that make it harder to — harder is not the right word — but often times, as you well know, vocals are overdubbed and you have more control over it so if he’s playing the piano at the same time it’s just another task for the engineer I guess.

items.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Ben Sidran, in his liner notes, draws out the comparison between your methods of operation and Thelonious Monk’s methods of operations

ctx.x: Well, it sounds like a lot.

We’ll do it in half-an-hour. It’s not that much. For Part 3, I’d like to return to some quotes from the past. There’s a 1972 recording called Mose In Your Ear. I thought this was an interesting remark. Ben Sidran, in his liner notes, draws out the comparison between your methods of operation and Thelonious Monk’s methods of operations, which he perceives.
